articles.title: Trump renames Lake Ontario ‘Lake America’ amid intensifying US-Canada trade dispute
articles.summary: President Donald Trump signed an order to rename Lake Ontario as 'Lake America,' asserting the U.S. holds most of its volume as trade tensions with Canada escalate.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Thursday signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America, a move that came amid a trade war with Canada. "The Lake of America was something I've been thinking about for a long time, actually. As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico — we changed it — and now it's very routinely the Gulf of America," Trump said in the Oval Office. The president said he has directed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and the department to update the Geographic Names Information System to reflect the name change. TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED The order called Lake Ontario a "tremendous asset" to the United States. "The United States is the greatest protector of the Great Lakes, including the body of water currently known as Lake Ontario," the order states. "Without the security and investment provided by the United States, this freshwater system would not be open for shipping, recreation, and responsible use to the same extent as it is today." The order said the U.S. Coast Guard supplies nine of the 11 ice-breaking vessels on the Great Lakes, securing commercial shipping lanes free of charge. The U.S. has also invested nearly $4 billion in protecting the Great Lakes freshwater ecosystem in the last decade, while Canada "has invested far less in similar initiatives over the same period." The move to rename the lake, which sits on the U.S.-Canada border, came amid a breakdown in trade between both nations, with Trump accusing Ottawa of unfair trade practices. OPINION: TRUMP MUST CLOSE THE BACK DOOR CHINA USES TO EXPLOIT NORTH AMERICAN TRADE Trump floated renaming Lake Ontario, one of the Great Lakes, hours before Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's announcement of reciprocal tariffs on U.S. imports. The U.S. imposed new 50% tariffs on Canadian goods such as wine, furniture and dairy products, while Carney said U.S. trade demands proved Washington wanted to "destroy our major industries," including autos, steel and aluminum, FOX Business previously reported. "Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade," Trump said Thursday. "Very sadly, even the military, you know, we defend Canada for nothing. We don't get anything. They don't pay us to defend Canada." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He said that Canada wants to "be treated like a state" and "we just can't do that anymore." Trump angered Canadian officials last year when he advocated for Canada to become the 51st U.S. state. Trump even jokingly floated renaming the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. "So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake," he said. "Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both." Trump previously used geographic names to make political statements, ordering the renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Ohio bakery workers recount surprise JD Vance encounter that took an unexpected turn
articles.summary: JD Vance invited three employees at Central Pastry Shop to ride in his motorcade to the Cleveland-Cliffs steel mill rally in Middletown, Ohio.
articles.body: When Vice President JD Vance stopped in at his hometown bakery last Friday, the last thing Cristaliz Portalatin expected was for him to invite her to his upcoming rally. But before she knew it, Portalatin and two of her fellow Central Pastry Shop employees were piling into a car in Vance’s motorcade to watch him speak at the nearby steel mill in Middletown, Ohio. "We knew he was going to come into Middletown, so we assumed he was going to stop by the shop," Portalatin, 28, told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday. "That morning, I was praying, and I was like, 'You know, it'd be nice for him to stop by, we can take a picture and talk to him.'" Vance did indeed visit, first greeting the shop's owner, Vera Slamka, who made a joke about him "losing too much weight" since the last time they saw each other. The vice president laughed before ordering an "ugly," the shop's signature misshapen-glazed donut. He called them "the best donuts in the world." VICE PRESIDENT JD VANCE OPENS UP ABOUT HIS CATHOLIC FAITH AND RELATIONSHIP WITH GOD: 'I FELT AT HOME' After Vance took pictures with Slamka and the rest of the staff, Portalatin recalled making an offhand comment about wanting to see the vice president's speech. "It was a comment that I made when he was talking to Vera. I just said, 'I would like to see the speech.' And he just said, 'Do you want to come?' That came from him," Portalatin said. Portalatin, along with her coworkers Ursula Bush and Jennifer Coby, accepted the offer and got to ride in a car with one of Vance's staffers. "We were just like laughing and were taking videos," Portalatin said. "It was very fun. We were just really enjoying. And I think the people that were there with us were also enjoying us and our reaction." CNN PANEL SWOONS OVER JD VANCE'S GLOW-UP, ADMITS MEDIA BLITZ IS 'IMPRESSIVE' FOLLOWING 'THE VIEW' APPEARANCE After an eight-minute ride, the starstruck trio were led into the Cleveland-Cliffs steel mill and were seated immediately left of the stage Vance spoke from. His speech focused on the new $500 million federal grant for the facility, which Vance's grandfather worked at as a welder decades earlier. Cleveland-Cliffs will invest another $500 million. The public-private investment is aimed at strengthening the domestic steel supply chain and is estimated to create 2,300 jobs, according to the Department of Energy. Bush, 53, told Fox News Digital that it was "amazing" to watch Vance announce this revitalization of the steel plant because she too has had many family members who worked there, including her father, great-grandfather, great-grandmother and great-uncle. SECOND LADY USHA VANCE KEEPS 'OPEN MIND' AMID JD VANCE 2028 SPECULATION Bush said Vance came across as "genuine" and "personable." "I got that when I was talking to him. He didn't have to ask us to come with him. He didn't have to treat us as well as he treated us," she said. Another thing about Vance that "spoke volumes" about his character was his attentiveness to his new baby, Alec Neel Vance, who was born on July 19. "He told us a little story about how the baby slept for the first time and only woke up once that night," Bush said. "I have three kids that I took care of all by myself, and for him to know that the kid only woke up once, that to me meant a lot. That made him a real person to me." "It truly was an honor to do something that not a lot of people get to do. I really think God allowed that to happen to us. So I'm still excited. I'll probably be excited for the next lifetime," Portalatin said.

articles.title: Trump administration designates three far-left groups as violent terrorist networks under new sanctions
articles.summary: The Treasury Department sanctioned Palestine Action, Autistici Inventati and Masar Badil, freezing U.S. assets tied to violent far-left terror networks.
articles.body: The Treasury Department announced sanctions against three far-left international networks as part of the Trump administration’s crackdown on politically motivated violence. The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control took action against Autistici Inventati, an Italy-based nonprofit; Palestine Action, a U.K.-based organization which it designated a terrorist group; and Masar Badil, a Spain-based group that allegedly operates as a front for the Samidoun Palestinian Prisoner Solidarity Network, already sanctioned by the U.S. "Far-left extremists, their fronts and their enablers should be on notice: We will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Political terrorism has no place in our society, and we will continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated." RUBIO PUTS ENTIRE WORLD ON NOTICE AGAINST RISE OF 'POISONOUS' FAR-LEFT TERROR 'MASKED AS EQUALITY' Over the past year, Treasury Department officials have leveraged the powerful Office of Foreign Assets Control to investigate far-left nonprofits and activists, including Marxist influencer Hasan Piker and CodePink co-founders Medea Benjamin and Jodie Evans, for allegedly violating U.S. sanctions against Cuba. Piker, Benjamin and Evans have denied any wrongdoing, and they haven’t been charged with any crimes. The latest move comes amid wider coordinated interagency efforts against far-left groups. Yesterday, the State Department issued a report saying that Autistici Inventati provided services to overseas terrorist groups and violent far-left agitators, causing chaos in American cities, according to a memo obtained by Fox News Digital. The memo also revealed Portland-based Rose City Antifa, known for participating in riots and property destruction, is one of the U.S. groups that relied on Autistici Inventati tools and services. Earlier this summer, Spanish authorities arrested wealthy far-left financier Fergie Cox, the estranged heir of the Cox cable TV empire, for extradition to the U.S. as part of a Justice Department investigation into his alleged funding of organizations, including Palestine Action. Cox has denied any wrongdoing and is fighting extradition. The Treasury Department also sanctioned two officials of Masar Badil. The sanctions block the groups’ access to any property or property interests located in the U.S. or controlled by U.S. citizens. The sanctions also freeze any bank accounts these organizations might have in the U.S. and prevent American citizens from conducting financial transactions with the groups. FBI SNARES AN AMERICAN HEIR INDICTED FOR ALLEGEDLY BANKROLLING ANTI-COP, PRO-HAMAS COMMUNIST REVOLUTION Last year, the U.K. government sanctioned Palestine Action, criminalizing any U.K. involvement or support for the group. Founded in 2020, Palestine Action is known for aggressive campaigns against defense companies it believes is supporting Israel. Palestine Action has reportedly broken into facilities, occupied factories and destroyed equipment. U.K. government officials said the group caused more than $1.3 million in damages to an Elbit Systems facility. Huda Ammori, Palestine Action co-founder, denounced the sanctions in a message on the X social media platform. "As a Palestinian and Iraqi, the fact the country which destroyed both my homelands is calling me a terrorist, is beyond hypocritical," she said. "Trump is the antithesis to everything Palestine Action stands for." As for Masar Badil, the Treasury Department said the organization serves as a front for the Samidoun Palestinian Prisoner Solidarity Network, which the U.S. and Canada sanctioned in 2024 after Treasury said it serves as an international fundraiser for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, a U.S.-designated Foreign Terrorist Organization. TRUMP ADMIN ACCUSES HAMAS OF BACKING GAZA FLOTILLA, SANCTIONS ACTIVIST AND MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD NETWORKS The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine was designated a foreign terrorist organization after decades of international terrorist attacks, including airline hijackings in the 1960s and 1970s that killed more than 20 Americans. The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine received its foreign terrorist organization designation alongside Hamas, Hezbollah and Palestinian Islamic Jihad in 1997. "Organizations like Samidoun masquerade as charitable actors that claim to provide humanitarian support to those in need, yet in reality divert funds for much-needed assistance to support terrorist groups," Bradley Smith, then-Treasury acting under secretary for terrorism and financial intelligence, said in an October 2024 statement. "The United States, together with Canada and our like-minded partners, will continue to disrupt those who seek to finance the PFLP, Hamas and other terrorist organizations." Samidoun’s internal coordinator, Charlotte Kates, rushed to X to defend Palestine Action and Masar Badil shortly after Treasury announced the sanctions. "The U.S.' latest sanctions and designations are targeting Palestine Action and the @MasarBadil, attempting once again to bring the upsurge for Palestine to an end through criminalization and state terror," Kates posted. "The fact is: designations can't stop a resistance or a revolution." Masar Badil executive committee member Khaled Barakat told Fox News Digital in a statement that U.S. sanctions are part of Washington’s broader campaign against Palestinians, accusing the U.S. of working with Israel to suppress pro-Palestinian activism and criminalize those who organize or speak out in support of the Palestinian cause. "The Trump administration is the primary perpetrator of terror in the world, along with its closest friend and co-conspirator, Benjamin Netanyahu and the Zionist regime," Barakat said. "Rest assured, these sanctions will not quiet the voice of the Palestinian people, and our work and our movement will not be suppressed by state terror. The world knows it to be true: no sanctions will succeed in shoring up a declining empire. Palestine will be free, from the river to the sea." In a new report, "Building a Transnational Movement Around Armed Resistance Advocacy," published Wednesday by researchers at George Washington University's Program on Extremism, the authors said Masar Badil was directly involved in unrest on some campuses following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel, and has repeatedly made efforts to physically mobilize to protest Israel and U.S. involvement. FBI NABS 7 FOR ALLEGED 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE' TO PRESSURE UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN, BUSINESSES OVER ISRAEL TIES In addition to Palestine Action and Masar Badil, the Treasury Department sanctioned Autistici Inventati, saying the group provides services such as website hosting on foreign servers, encrypted email accounts and digital infrastructure to violent left-wing extremist groups, including sanctioned terrorist organizations such as the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, which was also designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization in 1997. Lara Burns, a former FBI special agent who is now the head of terrorism research at George Washington University’s Program on Extremism, detailed why the organizations sanctioned by the Treasury Department pose a dangerous threat. "These networks are driving concepts that terror activities — that murder — are acts of legitimate resistance that are somehow justified, and that is a scary concept," Burns told Fox News Digital. "The broader this message is and the farther this message reaches, the more normalized it becomes. And so, as these groups have been allowed to operate both here in the United States and abroad, the message has become louder." Organizations will operate under the cover of charity or activism to mask their true and potentially violent intentions, Burns said. She noted that if nonprofit organizations "are driving pro-terror agendas under that cover, then the federal government needs to take action against them." The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, Burns said, has stealthily shifted from full-blown terrorist attacks to influence operations under the guise of activism, prisoner campaigns and transnational support networks. articles.title: Trump signs executive order renaming Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’
articles.summary: The move comes as Trump and Canada have become embroiled in a trade war.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Thursday signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America.” The move comes amid the president’s repeated threats and taunts that he would do so amid his escalating trade war with Canada. “This is official, effective immediately,” Trump said after signing the order in the Oval Office. The president said he’d “filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else” for the name change. “We notified all of the various people that we have to notify. So we’ve done everything that you have to do, and this is official, effective immediately,” he said. The order says that with “the deepest parts of the Lake’s waters lying within United States territory, the United States claims most of the Lake’s volume,” and that the “Lake has long been an integral asset to American exploration, settlement, commerce, and defense.” Asked what message he was trying to send Canada by renaming the Great Lake, Trump said, “No message. As you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade.” “They don’t pay for anything, and they want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state,” Trump said. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted on X a short time after Trump’s action that the name predates Canada — and the U.S. “The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big’. The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” he wrote. “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always,” he wrote. Lake Ontario has been called Lake Ontario since at least the 1600s, and is the inspiration of the name for Canada’s most populous province, Ontario, which is home to Ottawa and Toronto. Trump made a similar move last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” The Interior Department and Google and Apple complied with that directive, while the rest of the world largely has not. Trump suggested Thursday other larger renamings could follow. “So, the lake change, Lake of America, was something I’ve been thinking about for a long time. Actually, as you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico. We changed it, and now it’s very routinely the Gulf of America. So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake,” he said. “Now, all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.” Canadian maritime attorney Marc Isaacs told NBC News this week that a U.S. move on a name change of Lake Ontario wouldn’t affect other countries, including Canada, saying that no officials in either country own the naming rights to the lake. “The Americans can call it whatever they want to call it,” Isaacs said. “It is Lake Ontario.” Canadian Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly shrugged off Trump’s initial threats to change the name earlier this week. “We’ll always call it Lake Ontario. Period,” she said. “We’re proud of our Great Lakes.”

articles.title: Jon Ossoff condemns Hasan Piker's rhetoric as streamer declares mainstream media 'crisis of credibility'
articles.summary: Hasan Piker fired back at Jon Ossoff, accusing the Georgia senator of being part of a "bought & sold political class" after his antisemitism rebuke.
articles.body: Hasan Piker is facing yet another Democratic lawmaker critic amid the fallout from comments he made on a stream last week, this time from Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga. Ossoff, who is Jewish, was recently asked about Piker's comments that suggested American Jews could bring violence on themselves for being too associated with support of Israel. The senator, through a spokesperson, told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution that he "unreservedly rejects reckless and dangerous rhetoric suggesting that policy advocacy invites violence against the Jewish community or any community." "American Jews and all Americans must have the freedom and security to speak out and petition their government without fear of reprisal," he added. ELISSA SLOTKIN CALLS OUT HASAN PIKER FOR BLAMING JEWISH AMERICANS TARGETED OVER THEIR ISRAEL VIEWS In response to Ossoff's condemnation, Piker declared a media "credibility crisis" and appeared to suggest that the Georgia lawmaker was part of a "bought & sold political class." Piker had previously praised Ossoff as a potential dark horse 2028 White House candidate. "i think jon ossoff's best strengths came from his lack of interest in attacking his left flank & focusing on trump's corruption & scandals instead," Piker wrote on X. "i said he was a dark horse because he's been smart enough to back restrictions on weapons transfers to israel at times regardless of his incredibly conservative voting track record otherwise." HASAN PIKER POINTS THE FINGER AT AIPAC AS DEMOCRATS SPEAK OUT AGAINST HIM "this is part of the reason why many zionist orgs in georgia that masquerade as jewish advocacy orgs have aggressively condemned the jewish senator at times and still dangle their endorsement over mike collins who has literal white nationalists ties," he added. Piker then shifted his focus to the wave of condemnations against him that started following his controversial remarks. HASAN PIKER IS BECOMING THE 'FACE OF THE PROGRESSIVE MOVEMENT,' FORMER DEMOCRATIC OPERATIVE WARNS "i just wish people were more truthful about this entire ordeal. the last 48 hr media frenzy is exactly why people don't trust institutions from corporate media to our bought & sold political class. most of these orgs, and plenty in the media will operate like lapdogs for aipac with no care or consideration for nuance, the truth or how the majority feels about anything," he wrote. "this crisis of credibility for msm has been beneficial for me personally as an independent media personality, but i still naively believe that these institutions are worth preserving and defending at a time when we have no consensus reality," Piker added. In a separate post, Piker criticized what he seemed to characterize as widespread calls for political figures to condemn him. "in 3 years we went from 'do you condemn hamas' to 'do you condemn hasan' and israel is still a belligerent entity that is causing destruction, goading trump into war with iran & prominent dems are focusing on a critic of trump and israel instead of trump and israel itself. fools," Piker wrote. EL-SAYED DISTANCES HIMSELF FROM HASAN PIKER AFTER DISTURBING REMARKS ABOUT JEWISH AMERICANS Several Democratic lawmakers have issued statements against Piker this week, including Cory Booker, D-N.J.; Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich.; and Jacky Rosen, D-Nev.; House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.; and Reps. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.; Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y.; Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla.; Brad Schneider, D-Ill.; Greg Stanton, D-Ariz.; and Hillary Scholten, D-Mich. The condemnations came after Piker told his viewers during a recent stream, "If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews." Rosen condemned the remarks as a "new low" for Piker, who she said had been "trafficking in antisemitic tropes for a while." She went on to say that by "blaming Jewish Americans for the violence and hate they're facing," Piker provided "an excuse to those perpetuating these anti-Jewish hate crimes." Jeffries said the claim that American Jews were "inviting violence against themselves is dangerous and antisemitic." "There is zero justification for threats against the safety of our Jewish brothers and sisters at a moment of rising hate," the House minority leader added. "We will fight the cancer of antisemitism with the fierce urgency of now." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who appeared alongside Piker during his campaign, appeared to distance himself from the streamer as the controversy unfolded, saying that "nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople." "I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past," El-Sayed wrote on X. articles.title: Out-of-this-world fix for data center backlash could be on NASA's horizon
articles.summary: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman says solar-powered AI data centers in Earth's orbit could solve America's fights over land, water and grid capacity.
articles.body: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is backing a once-futuristic answer to America’s fight over AI data centers: Move them into Earth's orbit. Isaacman said Wednesday that solar-powered facilities in space could tap the sun’s energy without competing for the land, water and grid capacity required by sprawling data centers proposed across the country. "Let’s take our data centers, put them in Earth orbit, take advantage of that free fusion reactor that’s out there for us and use that to ensure we do win the space race for sure, but the AI race, too," Isaacman said in an interview with Nexstar DC. Isaacman’s idea comes as voters push back on the data center boom. A Fox News poll this summer found 70% of voters oppose building AI data centers in their own area, while 79% said construction should slow to address environmental and community concerns rather than move as quickly as possible to maintain a competitive edge over China. TRUMP TO HONOR ARTEMIS II ASTRONAUTS WHO TRAVELED FARTHER FROM EARTH THAN ANY HUMANS IN HISTORY Half of those opposed said environmental issues, including energy and water use, pollution and noise, were their chief concern. The idea comes with its own engineering problems. AI chips produce immense heat, and satellites would have to release it through large radiators. Operators would also need cheap, reliable launches, radiation-resistant hardware and laser links fast enough to connect thousands of computers spread across orbit. That has not stopped companies from trying to turn the concept into a business. Google has called Project Suncatcher a "moonshot" to place its TPU chips on solar-powered satellites linked by lasers. It plans to launch two prototype satellites by early 2027 to test its hardware in orbit and determine whether the satellites can share data fast enough for AI workloads. PETER NAVARRO: TRUMP'S ARTEMIS VISION IS NOW FLYING — AND CHINA IS PAYING ATTENTION SpaceX is pursuing a more aggressive version. Its proposed AI1 satellite would stand about 98 feet tall, have a wingspan of roughly 246 feet and carry up to 175 kilowatts of average AI computers, according to the company. SpaceX says it is building a Texas factory intended to produce thousands of the satellites as early as late 2027. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Small-scale tests are already underway. Startup Starcloud launched a satellite carrying a Nvidia H100 chip in November and says it later ran a version of Google’s Gemini model and trained a small language model in space. Starcloud plans its first commercial mission, Starcloud-2, for 2027. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP SpaceX has also asked the Federal Communications Commission for authority to deploy as many as 1 million orbital data-center satellites between 500 and 2,000 kilometers above Earth. The satellites would use optical links to communicate with one another and SpaceX’s Starlink network. The FCC has accepted the application for review but has not approved the constellation.

articles.title: Trump floats renaming the Atlantic and Pacific oceans after rebranding historic lake
articles.summary: President Donald Trump joked the Atlantic and Pacific oceans could be next after signing the executive order renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America immediately.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Thursday signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario "Lake America," then joked that the Atlantic and Pacific oceans could be next. "As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it, and now it's very routinely the Gulf of America," Trump said. "So if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean," he continued. "So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both." VANCE SAYS CANADA FRIENDLIER TO CHINA ON TRADE THAN TO US: 'INSANITY' Trump declared the Lake Ontario change "official, effective immediately" while announcing the order. "And finally, it's the purpose of this more than anything else is we're going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario, effective immediately to Lake America," Trump said. "That's going to take place right now as I signed the order." ‘CAPTAIN CANADA’ FIREBRAND UNLOADS ON TRUMP WITH PROFANE ONE-LINER AS TRADE WAR ESCALATES The president said the administration had "filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else" and notified the relevant parties. "So we've done everything that you have to do. And this is official, effective immediately," Trump said. CANADA REPORTEDLY SCRAPS JOINT BRIDGE CELEBRATION WITH US AFTER TRUMP RENEWS TARIFF THREAT The order directs Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, working with the Board on Geographic Names, to take steps within 30 days to rename the lake in the federal Geographic Names Information System and remove references to "Lake Ontario." It also directs the board to ensure federal maps, contracts, documents and agency communications use the new name. TRUMP BLAMES CANADA FOR WILDFIRE SMOKE, SAYS POLLUTION COSTS SHOULD BE ADDED TO TARIFFS The order does not control the name used by Canada, which borders the lake along with New York. It is not Trump’s first effort to put an American stamp on a major body of water. On his first day back in office, Trump signed Executive Order 14172, "Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness," directing the federal government to use "Gulf of America" in place of the Gulf of Mexico. TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED Trump later signed a proclamation declaring Feb. 9, 2025, the first "Gulf of America Day" while aboard Air Force One over the newly renamed gulf en route to Super Bowl LIX in New Orleans. "Today, I am very honored to recognize February 9, 2025, as the first ever Gulf of America Day," Trump wrote in the proclamation. CHAD WOLF: CANADA CAN'T EXPECT FREE TRADE WHILE LEAVING OUR NORTHERN BORDER VULNERABLE Burgum said at the time that the Interior Department had implemented Trump’s instruction from the executive order. The Lake America order invokes that same policy, arguing that the United States is the "greatest protector" of the Great Lakes system. It points to nearly $4 billion in U.S. freshwater ecosystem investment over the last decade, as well as the Coast Guard’s fleet of icebreaking vessels. SENATORS REJECT TRUMP’S CALL TO MAKE CANADA PAY FOR WILDFIRE SMOKE: ‘RIDICULOUS’ "The United States has invested nearly $4 billion in protecting the Great Lakes freshwater ecosystem in the last decade, while Canada has invested far less in similar initiatives over the same period," the order states. The order also cites the lake’s historic role in American trade, settlement, defense, commerce and energy, arguing it remains a major economic and strategic resource for the United States. "In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation’s economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America," Trump wrote. articles.title: Trump keeps winning Republican primaries; his losses may be more revealing
articles.summary: The president is 24-for-24 in Senate primaries and 214-for-218 in House races, according to a Fox News tracker
articles.body: President Donald Trump took to social media ahead of the latest round of Republican primary elections to emphasize, "My Endorsements are stronger than ever....There has never been anything close!" The numbers back up the president's assertions that despite some setbacks, he remains the ultimate kingmaker in GOP nomination showdowns. According to a Fox News Trump Primary Endorsement Tracker, the president is batting a thousand in Senate primaries so far this cycle, with all 24 of his endorsed candidates winning their contests. In House races, Trump has a nearly perfect record, with 214 of the 218 candidates he endorsed winning their primaries. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB In gubernatorial showdowns, Trump-backed candidates have suffered a handful of high-profile defeats, but overall, 16 of the 21 contenders for governor the president has endorsed have captured the party's nomination. This week, Trump-backed candidates scored statewide victories in two very competitive contests. Trump-endorsed Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina, who was recently appointed to fill the remaining months of her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham's current term, edged conservative Rep. Ralph Norman in a runoff to win the GOP Senate nomination for November's election. Graham will face the Democratic nominee in November in the race for the final months of her late brother’s Senate term. WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM RACES SHOW In Oklahoma, former state budget secretary and former state Sen. Mike Mazzei captured the GOP gubernatorial nomination by just 2,000 votes over rival Gentner Drummond, the state attorney general. "I supported and ENDORSED two so-called 'underdogs' yesterday, one from South Carolina, and the other from Oklahoma, and they BOTH WON," the president posted on social media Wednesday, following Tuesday's primaries. The president pulled out all the stops to help push Graham, whose stumble over international affairs during a debate last week grabbed national attention, over the finish line. Trump headlined a rally for Graham on Friday in Myrtle Beach, where he pledged federal funding for a long proposed new interstate highway in South Carolina. He also held a tele-rally for her on the eve of the primary. And MAGA Inc, the top Trump-aligned super PAC, dished out nearly $900,000 to support Graham's campaign. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER But the Trump endorsement hasn't proven to be a sure bet this cycle in South Carolina. Trump backed Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette for the GOP gubernatorial nomination — in the race to succeed the term-limited McMaster — ahead of the state's early June primary. Evette was the top vote-getter in the primary but lost the ensuing runoff election against South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson in a landslide. And Trump, ever hungry for a victory, endorsed Wilson in addition to Evette days before the runoff. It's undeniable that Trump has dramatically reshaped the GOP since his first White House victory a decade ago, with the populist MAGA and America First wings gaining prominence over more traditional fiscal and social conservatives. And the president's grip over party politics remains extremely firm. But he has had some setbacks, with five of his gubernatorial picks in Republican primaries this year going down to defeat. Besides South Carolina's Evette, that list includes Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones and Rep. Randy Feenstra of Iowa, who lost nominating contests this spring. And two weeks ago, Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder and Minnesota businessman and "My Pillow" founder and former CEO Mike Lindell fell short. HEAD HERE FOR THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLLS IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Meanwhile, two House incumbents endorsed by the president also lost their bids for renomination this month: Reps. Andy Ogles of Tennessee and Cory Mills of Florida, who was facing multiple controversies. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The Republican Party is Trump’s party, and there’s no question that an endorsement from the president provides a tremendous boost in a Republican primary. But it doesn’t necessarily mean the candidate’s going to win," veteran GOP strategist and communicator Ryan Williams told Fox News Digital. Williams said that "the president still has a firm grip on the party, even in places where a candidate he backed loses a nomination." But he noted that "if there are underlying issues with a candidacy, those can pose problems that even an endorsement can’t overcome."

articles.title: From Netflix to GPS: 10 ways this hidden tech infrastructure quietly powers modern life
articles.summary: Data centers power everything from streaming and gaming to AI chatbots and fraud detection. Here's how they quietly run the apps you use daily.
articles.body: Data centers are the hidden infrastructure behind much of modern life, powering everything from the apps on your phone and the shows you stream to online shopping, banking and artificial intelligence. Inside these warehouse-sized facilities, thousands of servers store data, process digital requests and keep online services running around the clock. Most Americans may never see one, but they use them constantly—often without realizing it. A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES "Anytime you’re touching technology and using everything from social media to your email, all of that information, all of the data is being processed in a data center," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital. The recent race to build more facilities is being driven in large part by AI, which Kaiser said processes "way more data" than routine activities such as email and social media. But data centers are necessary for so much more than creating a speedy reply to your ChatGPT questions. Here are 10 ways data centers quietly power the services Americans rely on every day. 1. They make your favorite apps work From Instagram and TikTok to Gmail and banking apps, data centers process and store the information behind the services people use every day. When you open an app, upload a photo, refresh your feed or send a message, your phone is connecting to servers that retrieve and deliver that information in seconds. The apps may live on a screen in your hand, but much of the work happens far away inside a physical facility filled with computers running continuously. 2. They keep your streaming and gaming smooth Netflix, YouTube, Spotify and other streaming platforms rely on massive computing infrastructure to deliver movies, videos and music to millions of users at once. Data centers help store enormous libraries of content and move it quickly enough to prevent the pauses and buffering that frustrate viewers. Online games also rely on data centers to connect players, synchronize what is happening in a match and reduce the lag that can make a game unplayable. The more people stream, game and use data-heavy services, the more computing power those platforms need behind the scenes. 3. They power AI tools Every time someone asks an AI chatbot a question, generates an image or uses an AI-powered search feature, data centers provide the computing power working behind the screen. Those requests require far more processing than a basic web search because the systems must analyze information and generate a response in real time. ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM That is a major reason the technology industry is racing to build bigger and more powerful data centers, often equipped with specialized chips designed for AI workloads. 4. They store your photos and files Your iPhone photos, Google Drive documents and cloud backups do not just float around in cyberspace. They are stored on physical servers inside data centers, often with copies kept in multiple locations to help prevent data loss. That means a lost phone or broken laptop does not necessarily mean lost memories or work files—but it also means the cloud depends on vast amounts of real-world hardware. 5. They help Google answer your questions instantly Search engines rely on data centers to sort through enormous amounts of information and return results in fractions of a second. Every query triggers systems that locate relevant webpages, images, maps, videos and other information before sending the results back to your device. What feels like a simple Google search is actually a complex exchange between your device and powerful servers processing requests at enormous scale. 6. They make online shopping possible When you order something online, data centers help manage inventory, process payments, make product recommendations and track packages to your door. They also allow retailers to update product availability and pricing quickly as demand changes. During major shopping events such as Black Friday, those systems have to handle a surge of shoppers and transactions without crashing. 7. They keep GPS and navigation running Google Maps, Waze and other navigation services depend on computing infrastructure to process traffic patterns, routes and location data in real time. They combine information from roads, users, businesses and mapping systems to estimate travel times and suggest alternate routes. Without the data centers behind them, navigation apps would not be able to react as quickly to accidents, congestion or changing road conditions. 8. They make remote work possible Video calls, cloud-based software, shared documents and workplace messaging all rely heavily on data-center infrastructure. Every Zoom meeting, Slack message and live edit to a shared file depends on servers that keep information synced between people working from different locations. For many companies, data centers have become as essential to day-to-day operations as office space, phones and electricity. 9. They help businesses detect fraud Banks, credit-card companies and retailers use powerful computing systems to flag suspicious transactions, verify purchases and help protect customers from fraud. Those systems can compare a purchase against patterns such as location, spending history and past transactions in a matter of seconds. KEVIN O'LEARY WARNS CHINA IS WINNING THE AI RACE BECAUSE U.S. STATES ARE SLOWING DATA CENTER PRODUCTION And that speed matters because a delayed fraud alert can give someone using a stolen card time to rack up multiple charges before the customer or bank can stop it. 10. They power the next generation of technology Autonomous vehicles, advanced robotics, scientific research and other emerging technologies require increasingly powerful computing infrastructure. Data centers help train the AI systems behind those tools, process huge volumes of data and support the software that allows them to improve over time. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As more parts of the economy become digital, the data center is becoming less of a niche tech facility and more of the infrastructure supporting modern American life.

articles.title: Trump executive order bans some foreign equipment in US energy grid
articles.summary: Order declares a national emergency over an ‘unusual and extraordinary foreign threat’ to the grid.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has declared a national emergency over what his administration describes as security risks linked to foreign-made equipment used in the US electricity grid.

Trump signed an executive order on Wednesday that restricts the purchase and installation of certain foreign-produced equipment used in the bulk-power system.

The order cited an “unusual and extraordinary foreign threat” from foreign-made systems, saying they could create vulnerabilities for US national security.

The directive targets certain bulk-power system equipment as well as related software and digital capabilities that the Trump administration said could create cybersecurity or operational risks.

The Department of Energy has 120 days to publish formal rules implementing the policy. In the meantime, experts are watching utility companies, which face the enormous task of compiling an inventory list of equipment flagged by the Trump administration.

“Blocking new purchases is the easy part. Knowing what’s already running is where the real work starts,” John Bruggeman, virtual chief information security officer of the telecommunications company CBTS, told Al Jazeera. “Utilities running foreign-sourced grid equipment … have a live compliance clock starting today.”

The move is the latest effort by the White House to address potential foreign security threats against the grid. Last year, US experts reported finding undisclosed communication devices in some Chinese solar power inverters. In July, the Federal Communications Commission banned all new foreign-made power inverters designed with remote communication capabilities and operating within the electric utility grid.

Still, the order does not prohibit all foreign-made equipment used in the US electricity system. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has been directed to establish conditions for the continued use and operation of affected equipment.

“The executive order establishes the authority to act,” Michael Centrella at the cybersecurity company SecurityScorecard, told Al Jazeera. “The difficult next step will be giving operators scalable, independent visibility into which assets and vendor relationships present the greatest risk without disrupting the reliability of the power system.”
